summary: Two sibling clauses in the same information sheet give conflicting procedural treatment to the identical conduct (a tenant assigning or subletting contrary to the lease), without ever flagging the overlap to the reader.

summary: The clause's generalization that a claim 'falling within one of these three preserved categories is not displaced by CUTSA merely because the same underlying facts could also support a trade secret misappropriation claim' is in real tension with the sibling case-law clause's own account of K.C. Multimedia, which holds that fact overlap (the 'same nucleus of facts') is precisely the test used to find a nominally non-trade-secret civil claim preempted.
evidence: Primary clause: 'a claim falling within one of these three preserved categories is not displaced by CUTSA merely because the same underlying facts could also support a trade secret misappropriation claim.' Sibling clause (cutsapreempt_case_law_same_nucleus_of_facts_test): 'the California Court of Appeal held that section 3426.7, subdivision (b), preempts common-law claims that are based on the same nucleus of facts as a trade secret misappropriation claim ... whether a particular non-trade-secret civil claim survives alongside a trade secret misappropriation claim can turn on whether that claim rests on facts distinct from the misappropriation, or instead restates the same underlying factual allegations under a different legal label.' The underlying opinion itself (K.C. Multimedia v. Bank of America Technology & Operations, CourtListener cluster 2256761) confirms this: 'we interpret the California statute as preempting claims based on the same nucleus of facts as trade secret misappropriation. Applying that construction to the operative pleading here, we agree with the trial court's conclusion that appellant's claims for breach of confidence, interference with contract, and statutory unfair competition are all preempted by CUTSA.' A reader of the primary clause alone would reasonably conclude that fact overlap is irrelevant to whether a category-(2) 'other civil remedies' claim survives, which is the opposite of what the controlling case law (quoted in this same document) actually holds for that category.
suggestedFix: Qualify the sentence by category: 'Categories (1) and (3) -- contractual and criminal remedies -- are preserved "whether or not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret," so fact overlap with a trade secret claim does not disqualify them. Category (2), "other civil remedies," is preserved only if the claim is not itself "based upon misappropriation of a trade secret" -- and California courts (see the companion clause on the "same nucleus of facts" test) decide that question by asking whether the claim rests on the same facts as the misappropriation claim. A category-(2) claim resting on the same nucleus of facts as a misappropriation claim is not preserved merely because it is pleaded under a different legal label.'

Independent publisher law.onecle.com's text of the same subdivision (reflecting the section as last amended by Stats. 2008, Ch. 177, Sec. 1): "This section applies to any domestic corporation and also to a foreign corporation having its principal executive office in this state or customarily holding meetings of its board in this state." The words "executive" and the phrase "in this state" (vs. "in California") differ between the two.
sourceChecked: https://law.onecle.com/california/corporations/1501.html (fetched this session); https://california.public.law/codes/ca_corp_code_section_1501 (a 2025-dated mirror of leginfo, not independent, which does match the clause's quoted wording exactly); leginfo.legislature.ca.gov itself returned a Cloudflare bot-check page on every attempt this session and could not be read directly without crossing into disallowed bot-check-circumvention techniques
suggestedFix: n/a - recheck the live leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text of Corp. Code § 1501(g) directly (not through a mirror) and confirm whether the operative language is "principal executive office in this state" or "principal office in California" before relying on either wording verbatim. onecle's copy may simply be a stale (circa-2018) snapshot that predates a later non-substantive revision, which would mean the clause is already correct, but that could not be confirmed independently this session.

summary: Stein v. hhgregg is cited for a 'deduction for unreturned property' rule, but the case actually involves clawing back a sales-commission draw/advance at termination, not a deduction for unreturned company property.
evidence: Stein, as fetched from CourtListener: 'if an individual is paid a $290 draw for a week in which she earns no commission, and is unable to earn in excess of $290 for any subsequent week, she would, upon termination, be required to return the $290 draw already paid to her. This aspect of the policy does violate the "free and clear" regulation, because it requires a repayment of wages already delivered to her.' Clause body: '{{companyName}} may ask {{employeeName}} to pay for property that isn't returned, but can't simply withhold its estimated value from {{employeeName}}'s wages... Federal law treats that kind of deduction the same as requiring an employee to hand wages back to the employer.'
suggestedFix: Either note that Stein involved a commission-draw clawback (not a property-deduction case) and is cited only by analogy for the 'free and clear' / anti-kickback principle under 29 C.F.R. 531.35, or replace/supplement with a case whose facts actually involve a deduction for unreturned employer property (e.g., a tools/uniform-deposit case) if one can be located.

summary: The clause states Quillian's 'bonus reduced by shortages violates the bond statutes' holding without disclosing that the California Supreme Court's later decision in Prachasaisoradej v. Ralphs Grocery Co. (2007) 42 Cal.4th 217 expressly distinguished and cabined that line of authority, holding that a genuine profit-based incentive compensation plan that subtracts store-wide expenses (including cash/merchandise shortages and workers' comp costs) to arrive at an overall profit figure does NOT violate Labor Code sections 400-410, 221, or 3751, and disapproving the Court of Appeal decision (Ralphs Grocery Co. v. Superior Court) that had extended Quillian's reasoning to that kind of plan.
evidence: Clause body/title: "the bonus herein is in contravention of the public policy expressed in sections 400 to 410 of the Labor Code pertaining to cash bonds that may be required of employees" and "a contract provision founded upon such act is void." Contrast with Prachasaisoradej v. Ralphs Grocery Co. (2007) 42 Cal.4th 217, 238-239, 245: "Quillian and Hudgins cannot be read for the premise that a plan of this kind fails on grounds the relevant 'profit' is measured, in accordance with common understanding, by subtracting expenses from revenues." ... "Though Ralphs Grocery did not expressly disagree with Quillian, supra, 96 Cal.App.3d 156, as to the rights of managerial employees, the two decisions are at odds on the point." ... "We will also disapprove Ralphs Grocery, supra, 112 Cal.App.4th 1090, to the extent it reaches contrary conclusions."
suggestedFix: Add to the clause's gap/body a disclosure along the lines of: 'The California Supreme Court's decision in Prachasaisoradej v. Ralphs Grocery Co. (2007) 42 Cal.4th 217 significantly limits Quillian's reach: it holds that a profit-sharing incentive compensation plan that subtracts store-level expenses — including cash and merchandise shortages and workers' compensation costs — when computing an overall store profit figure does not violate Labor Code sections 400 through 410, 221, or 3751, and it disapproved the Court of Appeal decision that had extended Quillian-style reasoning to such plans. Quillian's rule remains strongest for a formula, like the one at issue there, that assesses shortages dollar-for-dollar against a single employee's individually-calculated, sales-based bonus; it should not be read to invalidate every incentive plan that factors shortage or loss figures into a broader profitability calculation.'

summary: The clause's gap field incorrectly claims CourtListener's copy of In re Marriage of Rosevear (65 Cal.App.4th 673) is 'mis-linked to an unrelated New York decision' and therefore unfetchable, when the opinion is in fact reachable and resolves correctly through CourtListener's own citation lookup.
evidence: Clause gap text: "Rosevear itself was not fetched for this document (CourtListener's copy of that opinion is mis-linked to an unrelated New York decision)..." Live check: the official citation redirect https://www.courtlistener.com/c/cal-app-4th/65/673/ returns HTTP 302 to https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5808172/rosevear-v-rosevear/, whose text reads: "Section 2122 sets out the exclusive grounds and time limits for an action or motion to set aside a marital dissolution judgment," which is exactly the proposition Kieturakis quotes from Rosevear at 684. (Separately, a keyword search for "Rosevear" does surface an unrelated out-of-state case captioned "Rosevear v. Rees" -- but that is a 1955 Idaho Supreme Court decision, not a New York one, and it is not what the 65 Cal.App.4th 673 citation redirect resolves to.)
suggestedFix: Remove or correct the gap sentence claiming Rosevear is unreachable due to mis-linking. Rosevear v. Rosevear (In re Marriage of Rosevear) is reachable via CourtListener's citation redirect for 65 Cal.App.4th 673 and independently confirms the Kieturakis quotation; the document should either fetch and cite it directly or, at minimum, drop the inaccurate unreachability claim from the gap disclosure so future reviewers do not rely on a false premise about source availability.
